catalog_quote: Tuwuli has a fairly typical phonemic inventory for a Kwa language, with 21 consonants and 12 vowels (seven oral, five nasal). There are two basic (lexical) tone levels, high and low, which interact to generate at least four further tones phonetically, including a word-final falling tone. As with most other West African Niger-Congo languages, tone is also used to make several grammatical distinctions, especially distinctions of tense-aspect-mood (TAM) marking and polarity. The vast majority of syllables are open, with N, V, CV or CLV structure, although CVN syllables do occur in some adverbs and ideophones, as well as in a few common loanwords. [p. 76] ... Some clausal constituents can also be marked for focus in their default clausal position by means of a pitch-accent. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Tuwuli is a two-tone (H/L) language with phonetically derived tones including a word-final fall; no word-level stress is described. The only prominence phenomenon reported is a pragmatic focus 'pitch accent' realised on the focussed constituent (raised tonal contour, optionally raised intensity), i.e. phrase-level and not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Focus pitch accent is weaker or absent sentence-finally because downdrift obscures tonal distinctions (p. 84); tone patterns on day-names vary between speakers (fn. 6).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: lexical tone. The 'pitch accent' is a focus marker on clausal constituents (subjects especially), measured on sentences ('Kofi will come tomorrow'), so it is phrase/utterance-level prominence, not word stress. The source is a syntax/pragmatics paper by the author of the unread 553-page grammar; it does not address whether the word has stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuwuli is the autodenomination (people Bawuli, area Luwuli); Bowiri/Bowili/Bowuri/Boviri/Tuwili are exonyms for the same language (Harley 2009: 75 fn. 1). Höftmann 1966-67 and Westermann 1922 use 'Bowiri'/'Bowili'. No dialect division is mentioned in any source seen; all refer to tuwu1238.

sources.note: Sect. 1 'Typological characteristics' (p. 76): two basic lexical tone levels H and L, at least four further phonetic tones incl. word-final falling tone, grammatical tone for TAM and polarity; 21 C, 12 V, mostly open syllables. Sect. 2.4 (pp. 83-84): in-situ focus is marked by a 'pitch accent' = distinctly raised tonal contour on the focussed constituent, optionally increased intensity, with neighbouring tonal contours suppressed (Praat pitch/intensity figures). No statement about word stress anywhere.

sources.note: Sect. 1 'Tuwuli typology' (p. 122): seven-vowel system with cross-height root-controlled ATR harmony, five nasal vowels, limited labial harmony; subjunctive marked by low tone on the pronominal clitic. Nothing on stress (the single word 'stress' on p. 127 refers to English sentences).
Names, classification and speaker numbers only; no phonology.
